_readme: Sentence-judge golden set (TD-20, D53). Frozen: items are only ever appended (founder sentences via `python src/evals sentences import`), never edited. origin: native = published quotation (gold natural), seeded = one deliberate error (gold wrong), borderline = gold set by the founder's blind label, founder = written by the founder, gold set by an independent blind rater. expected = the author's or source's answer; where the founder's label disagrees on native/seeded items, the item is flagged and left out of scoring until resolved. synthetic = written by Claude Code imitating an advanced speaker's slips (founder 2026-10-01: stand-in for founder sentences for now); expected is Claude's label, provisional like the borderline items until a human confirms.

items.sentence: Investors were adamant on getting their money back by Friday.
items.note: adamant about / adamant that, not 'on'

items.sentence: The company curtailed its prices to win back customers.
items.note: you cut or lower prices; curtail spending or services

items.sentence: Her report bolstered a strong impression on the committee.
items.note: you make an impression; bolster supports something existing

items.sentence: We need to mitigate the gap between rich and poor districts.
items.note: narrow/close a gap; mitigate risks, effects, damage

items.sentence: The team reached a windfall when the sponsor doubled its budget.
items.note: you get/receive a windfall, not reach one

items.sentence: He has a deep acumen in marketing.
items.note: keen/sharp acumen, or marketing acumen; 'deep acumen in' is not idiomatic

items.sentence: Her scathing praise of the new chef made him blush with pride.
items.note: scathing means harshly critical

items.sentence: We were thrilled by the windfall of bad news from the hospital.
items.note: a windfall is an unexpected gain, never bad news

items.sentence: The nurse's perfunctory care saved my father's life; she checked on him every hour with real devotion.
items.note: perfunctory means done with minimal effort or interest

items.sentence: Grandma placated us with a delicious dinner to celebrate our graduation.
items.note: placate means calming someone who is angry

items.sentence: He disparaged his best friend at the wedding with a warm, glowing toast.
items.note: disparage means belittle

items.sentence: The dictator's affable crackdown left hundreds in prison.
items.note: affable means friendly and easy to talk to

items.sentence: She squandered her savings on a house, a smart investment that tripled in value.
items.note: squander means waste

items.sentence: The doctor told me to extrapolate the splinter carefully with tweezers.
items.note: confused with extract

items.sentence: I need to corroborate with my team before I give you an answer.
items.note: confused with collaborate/consult

items.sentence: The heavy rain began to coalesce the streets.
items.note: coalesce means come together into one; intransitive

items.sentence: My hindsight told me the bridge would collapse, so I took another road.
items.note: hindsight is understanding after the fact; confused with foresight

items.sentence: The new law will entrench on our freedom of speech.
items.note: confused with encroach on

items.sentence: The deadline is tenuous, so we must finish by 5 pm sharp.
items.note: tenuous means weak or flimsy; the meaning intended is strict/firm

items.sentence: The ubiquitous painting is the only one of its kind in the world.
items.note: ubiquitous means found everywhere

items.sentence: The witness's story was corroborate by two other people.
items.note: corroborated

items.sentence: She spoke with great candid about her illness.
items.note: candor (noun) needed, not candid (adjective)

items.sentence: Their strategy was very pragmatism, focused only on what would work.
items.note: pragmatic (adjective) needed

items.sentence: The negotiations reached impasse, and both sides walked out.
items.note: reached an impasse (article needed)

items.sentence: The teacher's speech galvanized, and the whole class signed up.
items.note: galvanize needs an object: galvanized the class

items.sentence: I have a propensity of losing my keys.
items.note: propensity for losing / propensity to lose

items.sentence: The report delineates about the new rules for drivers.
items.note: delineate takes a direct object: delineates the new rules

items.sentence: The meeting was quite convoluted, so I left early.
items.note: convoluted fits plans, plots, explanations; a meeting is 'long' or 'confusing'

items.sentence: She has a lot of gravitas for a student.
items.note: 'has real gravitas' is more usual than 'a lot of'

items.sentence: My boss gave me a caveat not to be late again.
items.note: a caveat is a qualification, not a warning to a person; may be wrong

items.sentence: The salient point of the movie is the ending.
items.note: salient = most noticeable; 'best part' is meant

items.sentence: I tried to assuage my hunger with a sandwich.
items.note: assuage hunger/thirst is attested, slightly literary

items.sentence: Prices have coalesced around $20 for most of these books.
items.note: figurative coalesce around a value; plausible

items.sentence: He is a very meticulous person in his cleaning.
items.note: 'meticulous about cleaning' / 'a meticulous cleaner'

items.sentence: This dichotomy between my two friends makes parties hard.
items.note: dichotomy = a split into two opposed categories, not a feud

items.sentence: We must underscore that the store will be closed on Monday.
items.note: formal but correct

items.sentence: The new manager's acumen is impressive in all things.
items.note: stiff; acumen is usually domain-specific (business acumen)

items.sentence: The interview felt a little perfunctory, like they had already chosen someone.
items.note: natural use

items.sentence: Her explanation was succinct, but it lacked details that were salient.
items.note: 'lacked the salient details' reads better

items.sentence: The ubiquitous use of phones in class is a pitfall for teachers.
items.note: a pitfall is a hidden danger in doing something; 'a challenge' is meant

items.sentence: His windfall of a promotion surprised everyone.
items.note: 'his unexpected promotion'; windfall is usually money

items.sentence: I'm adamant that you will like this restaurant.
items.note: adamant = refusing to change one's mind; for a prediction 'I'm sure'

items.sentence: Let's not belabor the details any longer; we need to decide now.
items.note: usual idiom is 'belabor the point'; 'the details' is acceptable

items.sentence: The pragmatic solution is to just call him.
items.note: natural

items.sentence: The project floundered a bit at the start, but it's doing well now.
items.note: natural

items.sentence: Her shrewd eyes were watching every move I made.
items.note: natural, slightly literary

items.sentence: There is a propensity among young people to use social media.
items.note: 'young people tend to'; propensity for something specific

items.sentence: Hey, can you delineate where you parked? I can't find the car.
items.note: register: far too formal for a casual message

items.sentence: Lol my cat totally eschewed her dinner tonight.
items.note: register and sense: eschew is deliberate avoidance on principle

items.sentence: Mom, please placate the baby, she won't stop crying.
items.note: register: soothe/calm the baby

items.sentence: Bro, that burger was the linchpin of my whole day.
items.note: register: playful; may read as deliberate humour

items.sentence: Text me the salient details of the party, like time and place.
items.note: register: formal word in a casual text

items.sentence: OMG, the zeitgeist at this party is amazing!
items.note: zeitgeist = spirit of an era; 'vibe' is meant

items.sentence: I'm going to curtail my nap today because I have homework.
items.note: register: 'cut my nap short'

items.sentence: The new hire really bolstered our team's morale during the crunch.
This decision could bolster the risk of a recession.
items.note: bolster strengthens something you want; 'raise the risk'

items.sentence: My manager was adamant in keeping the deadline.
items.note: adamant about keeping; 'adamant in his refusal' exists, so not flatly wrong

items.sentence: She faced a lot of adversities in her first year abroad.
items.note: adversity is usually uncountable: 'a lot of adversity'

items.sentence: I appreciated the candor of his feedback, even though it stung.
She talked with candor and told us all the gossip about her boss.
items.note: candor is frankness about your own views, not sharing gossip

items.sentence: We squandered two hours in traffic this morning.
items.note: squander implies wasting a resource through your own fault; 'lost two hours'

items.sentence: The scandal galvanized voters to come out in record numbers.
Can anyone corroborate that the meeting was moved to Thursday?
I eschewed the meeting because I was sick.
items.note: eschew = avoid deliberately, on principle; 'missed'

items.sentence: To placate the angry customer, the waiter offered a free dessert.
After the CEO left, the startup was floundering for direction.
items.note: 'floundering without direction' / 'searching for direction'

items.sentence: Choosing between the two job offers was a real conundrum for me.
We're at an impasse with the landlord about the deposit.
Winning the scholarship was a windfall for my career.
items.note: a windfall is luck, usually money; a scholarship is earned

items.sentence: She is the linchpin of our team; without her, nothing gets done.
His business acumen helped the company survive the downturn.
I'm in a quagmire about which laptop to buy.
items.note: quagmire = a messy situation hard to get out of; 'dilemma'

items.sentence: He made an astute decision to invest early.
The hotel staff were perfunctory and helpful.
items.note: perfunctory = minimal effort; contradicts 'helpful'

items.sentence: The link between the two events is tenuous at best.
The critic wrote a scathing review on the new restaurant.
items.note: a review of, not on

items.sentence: The interview was very affable, I felt relaxed.
items.note: affable describes people, not events

items.sentence: My grandmother was a shrewd woman who never overpaid for anything.
The diplomat deftly avoided answering the question.
The government curtailed the protesters from entering the square.
items.note: curtail limits an activity; 'prevented/barred the protesters from'

items.sentence: The contract clearly delineates the responsibilities of each party.
We can extrapolate from his silence that he disagrees.
items.note: infer is meant; extrapolate extends a trend

items.sentence: The report underscores on the need for better training.
items.note: underscore takes a direct object

items.sentence: Smartphones have entrenched in our daily lives.
items.note: become entrenched / entrenched themselves
